clauses.statement: computeCatalogIdentity applies 5.1's JCS rules to exactly {formatVersion, catalogVersion, resolvedFallbackLocale, localeToSha256, tiebreakers}, and catalogFingerprint is the lowercase hex SHA-256 of those JCS UTF-8 bytes.
clauses.ablation: S6 ran five ablations against the finished code; four fired, and the one that did NOT (making the canonicalizer SORT ARRAY ELEMENTS) was traced to a fixture whose only array was already sorted — the fixture became ["en-001","en"] and the ablation then turns the pinned canonical bytes red.
clauses.evidenceLine: CONFIRMED (re-check). M8-STATUS.md:412-416 verbatim: "Five ablations were run against the finished code; four turned the tests red and one did not: making the canonicalizer SORT ARRAY ELEMENTS changed nothing ... The fixture now uses ["en-001", "en"] ... and that ablation turns the pinned bytes red" — a real perturbation, performed, result stated. :397-401 four FIPS 180-4 vectors incl. the one-million-'a' message + node:crypto differential at every length 0-200 (55/56, 63/64, 119/120 boundaries); :407-411 one exclusion test per excluded field each with an included-field control; :426 pinned bytes as well as a pinned digest; :391 "908 -> 917 tests. verify exit 0, check exit 0". Gate is a TOOL, not a file: verified `verify` and `check` are real scripts (lokalized-js/package.json). WEAKNESS CONFIRMED: lines 387-435 name ZERO test files (grep for "test/" in that range returns nothing); test/catalog-identity.test.js and test/sha256.test.js exist on disk but the record never names them. Held PROVEN only because the governing rule admits a tool as the named gate.

clauses.statement: The catalog fingerprint EXCLUDES itself, the CLDR/data fingerprints, and transport-only baseUrl, url and decodedBytes, so server and CDN manifests identify the same translations.
clauses.ablation: THREE ablations, all firing. Adding `baseUrl` to the projection and adding `cldrVersion` to it each turn "clause 2: the projection keeps EXACTLY the five identity fields" red; folding the transport-only per-file `url` into the per-locale digest turns the two-origins test and the one-field-at-a-time test red. Control 5 tests / 0 failing before and after.
clauses.evidenceLine: MEASURED BLIND AT THE LAYER THAT ACTUALLY EXCLUDES: `computeCatalogIdentity` hashes whatever projection it is handed, and `src/load/identity.js:110` says so — it "cannot exclude `baseUrl` or a per-file `url`, because they never reach it: this is the function that drops them". The function that drops them is `catalogIdentityInputFor`, and nothing tested it: adding `baseUrl` to it turned ZERO tests red across eight files, and so did adding `cldrVersion`. Only the per-file `url` was gated, incidentally — folding it into the digest changes the hashed VALUE, which the pinned-bytes test catches for a reason unrelated to exclusion. AND THE WIDENING IS SILENT, so a widened projection changes no fingerprint and no behaviour, and the exact-key-set assertion is the only thing that can catch it. CORRECTED 2026-09-18: this read `the canonicalizer IGNORES a member it does not know (measured — {...the five, baseUrl} produces byte-identical output)`, and that named the wrong function. Executed against `canonicalBytes` itself, the output is NOT byte-identical — `baseUrl` is serialized in sorted position. The silent-widening property belongs to `projection()` (src/load/identity.js:76-83), which rebuilds the object field by field and drops what it was not taught. Same conclusion, different mechanism, and the difference is load-bearing: anyone reading the old sentence would conclude that widening the projection is free, where in fact `canonicalBytes` REFUSES an undefined member and the whole suite fails.

The loader does not emit these fields at all, which the new test asserts first, so the renderer is their only possible source. loaded-input.js:288-292 had said exactly this in a comment since S10 — "taking them from `loaded` would be indistinguishable now and wrong the moment that check is relaxed" — and nothing checked it.

clauses.statement: The manifest is self-versioned and digest-binds every body; production HTTP(S) URLs are immutable per catalog version; a dev file: manifest may point at scanned sources; service workers must not precache the whole catalog.
clauses.ablation: SIXTEEN ablations over 21 tests, all firing: the format version unchecked and then deleted; the fingerprint never compared; the per-file url folded into the identity projection (13 red); the runtime-data check dropped; `sha256` made optional; a digest mismatch downgraded to a warning; `decodedBytes` never planned; `Content-Length` compared; each door's scheme preflight removed; the url reconstructed from the tag; the identity taken from what loaded; and the validator's scheme check dropped and then narrowed to http. Method: blind design, adversarial refutation, then authoring with the repairs applied. All 51 ablations for this slice ran against a throwaway copy, control 96 tests / 0 failing.
clauses.evidenceLine: RECORDED WITH ITS LIMITS IN WRITING, because most of this clause is publisher discipline rather than library behaviour. What is gated: the manifest is self-versioned (format version and fingerprint both checked), every body is digest-bound (a mutated body at a stable URL is REFUSED rather than served, at three distinct plan positions), identity moves with a body, and a version-bearing publication base survives generation unmangled. What is NOT gated and is now said plainly: "immutable per catalog version" is a property of a deployment OVER TIME — the runtime never sees two publications of one version — and "service workers must not precache" is advice to an application, with no service worker in this package at all. The previous entry called the URL-shape half "the ONE mechanically checkable half", which OVERSTATED it: what is checkable is that the base is not mangled, not that the emitted URLs are digest-derived or versioned. Nothing enforces the latter, and the generator has no URL-mode option to enforce it with.

clauses.statement: The hashes give consistency and corruption detection, NOT authenticity against an attacker who can replace manifest and files; production guidance requires a trusted HTTPS origin or an app-owned signature.
clauses.ablation: Five ablations, all firing, control clean. Stopping the body-digest comparison reds 'tampering with the catalog BYTES alone is caught at the digest' AND takes check:readme to exit 1, so the README sample is a live gate on the check and not an illustration. DELETING THE WHOLE README SECURITY SECTION reds only 'the README carries the production guidance, and names both remedies' while check:readme stays at exit 0 with 41 groups — which is the measured proof that the presence assertion is the only thing that can see it, because check:readme's anti-vacuity terms are GLOBAL. Making the tampered body a DIFFERENT length reds both the same-length assertion and the tamper arm, which is the zh-123 guard working: at unequal length the load is refused at stage 'limit' and never reaches a hash. And adding one new caller option to src/load/ reds the derived option-surface assertion, which is what makes the staleness arm name-independent.
clauses.evidenceLine: CLOSED by M-D S18, and the premise it was held on is wrong. M8-PLAN.md:255's 'nothing executable' is false: the proposition is a PAIR of loads over one door with opposite outcomes. Measured — replace only the catalog bytes and the load is refused at stage 'digest'; replace the MANIFEST too and it succeeds and serves the attacker's words, because the manifest is the trust root and nothing in this library verifies it. Stripping a sha256 is a ConfigurationError and blanking one is refused by the manifest's own catalogFingerprint self-consistency check, so regenerating the whole manifest is the only route and it needs an untrusted channel. Both remedies the clause names are exercised rather than recommended: an https origin you trust, and pinning getCatalogIdentity().catalogFingerprint against a value the build carries out of band.

clauses.statement: Manifest fallback resolution: exact tag, else the sole CLDR-equivalent, else the first equivalent in the tiebreaker list; zero or ambiguous FAILS; the resolved tag never rewrites a direct request's lookupLocale.
clauses.ablation: The two arms are gated at the manifest door by C6 and C7, each asserting the refusal AND that no file is read: a recording transport sees ZERO calls where before the fix the zero-candidate case fetched every catalog and the ambiguous case fetched the elected one. Both also assert the PARSE door and the PLANNER, because an implementation that refused in validateStringsManifest and still elected inside chain/fetchSet would pass a validation-only test. Controls: the same files with an electable fallback validate, plan and load.
clauses.evidenceLine: CLOSED BY A MAINTAINER DECISION, and the divergence it removes was real rather than cosmetic. Plan 6.2:145 says zero or still-ambiguous matches fail construction AND MANIFEST VALIDATION; only the direct door implemented it. At the manifest door a fallback equivalent to two declared catalogs was SILENTLY ELECTED: chain() ended on the tag-sorted first, the subset door fetched that one file, and the instance served every unmatched request from a catalog nobody chose - a complete:true load of a manifest the plan says must be refused. The core guard that would have caught it is reachable only through the WHOLE-manifest door, which fetches both files first. Refused now at validation, before any per-file plan exists, for the reason S11a recorded one door over: inside the planner it degrades into one failure among many, and under allow-partial that is a successful load which skipped what the caller asked for. THE REMEDY IN THE MESSAGE WAS WRONG ON THE FIRST ATTEMPT AND A FIXTURE CAUGHT IT. It told the publisher to declare a manifest tiebreaker; validateManifestTiebreakers groups files by PRIMARY LANGUAGE and skips undetermined tags outright, so a tiebreaker keyed 'und' is itself refused. The message now says to spell the fallback as one of them exactly, and the test asserts BOTH that the remedy works and that the tiebreaker route does not.

Every ablation ran against a throwaway copy of the package; the harness was negative-tested four ways after being changed (absent anchor and ambiguous anchor report DID-NOT-LAND, a behaviour-preserving edit reports DID NOT FIRE, and an expected-red naming a nonexistent test is reported as such), control 132 tests / 0 failing.

The universal form is not claimed and is recorded as deferred: two schedules per door are sampled, not all interleavings. The designer's original fixture was MEASURED to throw ConfigurationError before planning and was respecified.

clauses.statement: The loaded branch of createStrings preserves LoadedStrings.warnings exactly, without resorting.
clauses.slice: S16 (probes) + S17 (the consistency refusal that makes the guarantee universal)
clauses.ablation: FIFTEEN ablations over 21 tests, all firing, controls clean on both sides. Nine against the preservation probes: sorting the replay by locale, by locale-then-key and by key; deduplicating; skipping the onWarning replay; re-stamping the source; sorting missingLanguageForms; handing out the internal array; and making the LOADER emit catalogs in an order other than fetch-plan order. Six against the consistency refusal: removing it entirely turns 5 red; comparing only the COUNTS turns the three ordering tests red and leaves the count test green; comparing only the FIRST pair turns exactly the later-index test red; comparing by object IDENTITY rather than by value turns the CONTROL red — which is what proves the value comparison is load-bearing, since every serialized record rebuilds its objects; defaulting a missing `warnings` field to [] turns the missing-field test red; and deriving the comparison from the aggregate itself — the tautology that can never disagree — turns 4 red.
clauses.evidenceLine: UPGRADED FROM NOT-PROVEN, and the mechanism is stated rather than glossed. The loaded branch still does not READ `loaded.warnings`: it hands `catalogs` to the shared construction path, which replays each ParsedStringsFile's warnings in catalogs-key order. What changed is that a record whose two copies of its own warning list disagree is now REFUSED at construction, so for every record that constructs, `getWarnings()` equals `loaded.warnings` exactly, by value. The clause's guarantee therefore holds UNIVERSALLY where it previously held only by coincidence — the coincidence being that `run-plan.js` builds `catalogs` and `warnings` from one slot walk. MEASURED BEFORE THE CHECK WAS WRITTEN, in an instrumented copy of the package across the whole suite, conformance and two differentials: 88 constructions from a loaded record, 0 disagreements, 0 source-field differences — but 77 of those 88 carried NO warnings, and all 11 that did came from the file written for this clause. Before this work the repository had never constructed from a loaded record carrying a warning, so 'nothing breaks' is thin evidence and is recorded as thin. The hazard is real rather than theoretical: a record survives JSON.stringify/parse and structuredClone intact (measured — that is the server-render path), but SORTING `catalogs` for deterministic output was accepted by every other check, since `requestedFiles` is untouched and the catalog SET is unchanged, and it silently changed the order `getWarnings()` reported while the record's own field said otherwise. Dropping a catalog was already refused by the coverage check; reordering was refused by nothing. WHETHER THE AGGREGATE IS AUTHORITATIVE OR DERIVED REMAINS A MAINTAINER QUESTION, deliberately not settled here — but it is now a question about internal design rather than about observable behaviour, and refusing the disagreement is what makes either answer safe to adopt later.

Every ablation was applied to a THROWAWAY COPY of the package, never to the working tree, and the harness itself was negative-tested four ways before its results were trusted: an absent anchor and an ambiguous anchor both report DID-NOT-LAND rather than a clean run, a behaviour-preserving edit reports DID NOT FIRE, and an expected-red naming a test that does not exist is reported as such.
